## What changed since the last chronicles (v3), and what is still to come

These three chronicles (v4, seeds 1–3) ran on the build of 2026-11-12 (commit 3b819fa). They are the first century runs where the colony's economy holds together, so you can read the material history as well as the politics.

### Changed since v3

**The economy survives a century (Bob)**
- **Farms get built again.** The real cause of the famines was a broken supply chain:
  1. The public utility took over the failed mining and smelting firms.
  2. Its smelters drew ore from its own stock, and that never counted as demand.
  3. So the mines idled at 20%, builders got no materials, and no farm was ever finished.

  Now a company's own plants count as demand.
- **Builders no longer collapse.**
  - Crews work on paid, overdue and nearly finished contracts first, instead of being spread thin and lost.
  - Each company has only one plant of a type under construction at a time.
  - A builder can win only contracts it can staff.
- **Population ages properly.**
  - Retirees used to live about 60 years in retirement. Now people live to about 78, less where healthcare is poor.
  - Births come from working-age adults.
  - Famine raises deaths in every age group.
  - A food shortage softly lowers births and new settlers.
- **Retirement age is a law** (default 62, from 55 to 72), so parties can fight over pensions against workers.
- **On-the-job training.**
  - Firms with skilled posts they can't fill pay workers to train one level up.
  - Schools make training faster.
  - Trainees earn more and move up in class over time.
  - A training subsidy and a training budget are laws parliament can pass.
- **Fabrication kits** (your proposal): the colony lands with a crude parts workshop and smelter that can be upgraded Mk I → III.
- **Bob's 6-colony century test:**
  - Famine in 1 of 6 colonies, where it was 6 of 6. Famine is still possible, as you wanted.
  - No colony defaults on its debts, where it was 5 of 6.
  - Population at year 100 is 2.3–2.6 thousand.

**Governments secure the essentials (your proposal)**
- Every quarter an AI government checks food, power, water, materials and components.
- **State-minded governments build** the plant themselves. State farms are run by a new Colony Agricultural Board.
- **Market-minded governments offer a grant** (about 25% of the cost, for 2 years) to any company that builds one.
- **Centrists offer the grant first, and build if the shortage persists.**
- Nothing is automatic. A government that won't act, or finds no taker, can starve the colony. When you govern, nothing is built behind your back.

**Elections**
- **Runaway landslides fixed.** New parties had a hidden head start that snowballed to 70–94% of the vote. The largest party now peaks around 46–51%, with 4–11 effective parties.
- **Election-year goodies** that voters discount if the party isn't believed.
- **Leaders' debates:** three questions on the most pressing concerns; leaders attack, defend or pivot, and may misjudge.
- **Party congresses** adopt manifestos and handle rebel motions. The campaign themes come from the congress. *This part is still being checked for causing too many party splits.*

**Newspapers (Anni and Wilma)**
- **Several papers.** The state Gazette, plus papers that unions, companies and parties can found.
  - Each picks and frames its own stories, and owners can bury their own bad news.
  - What people read shifts their mood, their issues, who they blame and, over years, their politics.
- **False reports.** Partisan papers print about 3 lies, errors or spin stories a year, about half of them exposed. Trust falls for papers that lie: the Gazette ended a test run at 70, the union paper at 53, the business paper at 39.
- **Defamation suits, press investigations, and censorship** (only in a state of emergency).

**In the game (not visible in this text)**
- An **Election Night** screen counts districts one by one into a 151-seat chamber.
- **The Gazette window** shows each paper's real-looking front page.
- **The 3D globe** shows the colony map lying on its landing hex, with storms over the colony.

### What this run shows (seed 3)
- **No famine, but the hardest economy:**
  - Real income falls to about 54–67 between Years 51 and 81 and recovers to about 89–99 by the end.
  - Public debt climbs to about 40–53% of GDP.
  - The home world raises the quota to 50% at a charter price of 65–80%: the colonial burden at its heaviest.
- **The most party churn:** 25 parties over the century, with 15 new parties and 14 mergers, and 11–13 in parliament. The largest party rarely tops 30 seats.
- **Unemployment** averages 19%, with peaks of 33% around Year 81.

### Known problems in this build
- **Long-run unemployment of 16–21% on average (23–34% by year 100).** The cause is too little demand, not a skills gap: skilled workers are out of work too.
  - Companies keep building plants the colony doesn't need. There's 2–9 times more materials capacity than demand.
  - Plants only hire for what they actually produce, so the extra machines create no jobs.
  - Bob is checking whether unemployment benefits keep spending up and whether investment stops at enough capacity. Wilma will broaden public works for governments that believe in them.
- **Party congresses** may cause too many party splits (2–12 active parties across test runs); Ella is checking with and without them.

- **Things the new systems don't do yet in these runs:**
  - Nobody founds a rival newspaper on their own, so only the state Gazette exists (unions and companies need a reason to start papers).
  - No government ever changes the retirement age.
  - No state farm was needed: food never fell short enough, though grants for new plants were offered 5–7 times on seeds 1–2.

### Still to come
- **Areas drive the economy.** Settlements already exist on the terrain map and split. Next, the economy runs per area rather than per old district, and districts are drawn by law on top.
- **Housing life-cycle** (your proposal): housing decays slowly at first, then fast, so old stock becomes cheap housing or slums. Expensive builds give better profits and widen divides. The state sells or leases its land.
- **Colonial goods:** the rare mineral and native crop, shipped as the home world's quota. Ship size follows the home world's demand and the colony's attractiveness, and people leave a colony that can't feed or house them.
- **Random crises and company greed:** epidemics, accidents, lost ships, speculative food crises and crashes. Greedy firms make them likelier, and hidden causes come out in inquiries.
- **Technology** isn't on the board yet. Climate warming stays barely noticeable until it is.
